name: Matthiessen's Rule
statement: The total electrical resistivity of a metal is the sum of contributions from independent, additive scattering mechanisms.
statementAccent: sum of contributions from independent, additive scattering mechanisms
meaning: Matthiessen's rule treats the different processes that scatter conduction electrons, such as thermal lattice vibrations and static impurities or defects, as acting independently. Because independent scattering rates add, the resistivities they produce also add. This separates a temperature-dependent phonon term from a temperature-independent residual term due to impurities and defects.
mechanism: Each scattering process has its own relaxation time, and independent processes contribute reciprocal relaxation rates that sum to give the total rate. Since resistivity is proportional to the total scattering rate, the resistivities add: total resistivity equals the phonon term (temperature-dependent) plus the impurity term. The phonon term rises with temperature while the impurity term stays roughly fixed.

examples.text: As a pure metal is cooled toward absolute zero, the phonon term vanishes and resistivity levels off at a residual value set by impurities and defects.
In silicon, carrier mobility is estimated by summing reciprocal mobilities from ionized-impurity and acoustic-phonon scattering.
Adding solute atoms to a metal raises the temperature-independent residual resistivity while leaving the phonon contribution largely unchanged.

whyItMatters: The rule provides a simple, widely used framework for decomposing measured resistivity into intrinsic and defect-related parts, and it underlies the use of residual-resistivity ratio as a purity metric. It is fundamental to interpreting electron transport in metals and semiconductors.
limits: It is an approximation valid only when scattering mechanisms are truly independent. It fails when processes are correlated — for example when phonon scattering alters electron velocities and thereby changes impurity scattering. Deviations appear in alloys, anisotropic metals, and at intermediate temperatures where the terms are not cleanly separable.
misreadings: Additivity of resistivities is a consequence of assumed independence, not a universal guarantee; observed deviations signal correlated scattering rather than a failure of measurement.
origin: Established by Augustus Matthiessen with Carl Vogt in "On the Influence of Temperature on the Electric Conducting-Power of Alloys", Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1864. Measuring alloys across a temperature range, Matthiessen found the resistivity separating into a temperature-dependent part belonging to the pure metal and a temperature-independent part belonging to the impurities — the additive split the rule is named for, arrived at experimentally some seventy years before the scattering theory that explains it.

sources.text: Matthiessen, A. & Vogt, C. (1864). "On the Influence of Temperature on the Electric Conducting-Power of Alloys." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London 154, p. 167.
